title: Isaiah 66:1–6
context: Heaven is his throne and earth his footstool; the house they would build cannot contain him. He looks to the humble, contrite, and those who tremble at his word. Formal sacrifice without that heart is like killing a man or blessing an idol. He called and no one answered. Those who tremble are hated and cast out by brothers who say, Let the Lord be glorified; a voice from the temple renders recompense. Historic Judah’s temple first, then the gospel church Stephen reads here (Acts 7:49).

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about heaven his throne, the contrite to whom he looks, and a voice from the temple.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The heaven is the place where I shew myself in my majesty. Hence we are taught to pray, Our Father which art in heaven. Can there be an house built that will contain me? Yet God will look with a favourable eye to him that hath a broken and contrite spirit, who trembleth when he hears God’s threatening words, and hears every revelation of his will with reverence. Solomon, Prov. xv. 8, gives a full commentary: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord. The prophet is not reflecting upon idolatrous worship, but formal worship: upon those who in a formality worshipped the true God by acts which he had appointed. They have chosen to mock and delude me; I will chuse to suffer them to delude themselves. You—that truly fear God. Your brethren—by nation—that cast you out of their synagogues, for my name’s sake, thinking they did God good service (John 16:2). A voice from the temple: thus he seems to express the destruction of the Jews by the Roman armies.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 66:1–6)

reformed.quote: He shews that they grossly mock God who endeavor to serve him by outward ceremonies. Heaven is my throne: his majesty fills all things; he is so far from being shut up in the temple that he is not confined within any place. Stephen quotes this (Acts 7:49). I look to him who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembleth at my word. True godliness consists in having our senses brought into obedience; all the reverence we owe to God must be paid to his word. He that killeth an ox as if he slew a man: he does not absolutely condemn sacrifices, but the blemishes of them, when men think God is satisfied with a deceitful appearance. I also will choose their delusions, because when I called they did not answer. Hear, ye who tremble: he arms believers against domestic foes who cast them out. A voice from the temple: they shall not escape his hand, and even from the temple, their lurking-place of false confidence, his voice shall come forth.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build to me? Where will I rest?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the highest heaven is the place where I shew myself in my majesty (Ps 11:4; 103:19; Matt 5:34). Hence we are taught to pray, Our Father which art in heaven. The earth is my footstool (Matt 5:35). Can there be an house built that will contain me? Where is the place wherein I can be said to rest in a proper sense?

The Father in heaven is not boxed in the temple. House first; Stephen (Acts 7:49) then the gospel church. Shared christology with Calvin: heaven his throne; he is a Spirit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they flattered themselves in sins under confidence in sacrifices and the temple. This confidence is diabolical; they frame an idol when they shut him up in the temple. Heaven is his throne so we may raise our minds above the world; yet he protests he is with us. Worship must be spiritual to correspond to his nature (John 4:24). Stephen (Acts 7:49) and Paul (Acts 17:24) apply it: God dwells not in temples made with hands.

He is not confined; ceremonies without the heart are a mockery. Same question, Where is the house?; the rest named in Psalm 132 is not a prison for his majesty.

verses.text: For my hand has made all these things, and so all these things came to be,” says the LORD: “but I will look to this man, even to he who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: they were not only made by God, but kept in being by him. Look—yet God will look with a favourable eye to him that hath a broken and contrite spirit, whose heart is subdued to the will of God, and who is poor and low in his own eyes. Trembleth—who trembleth when he hears God’s threatening words, and hears every revelation of his will with reverence.

The contrite may still be looked on; trembling at the word is reverence, not terror without hope. Judah; the gospel still looks to that man.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: ceremonies are empty when men think they satisfy God by them. He made all these things; he has no need of external worship (Ps 50:10). He looks to the humble, contrasted with the splendor of ceremonies. Trembling at the word is the obedience of those who reverence him, not the terror of those who flee. All reverence we owe to God must be paid to his word. Though wretched in abasement, we are happy because the Lord looks upon us.

“Look”—inward purity and the word, not the array of the house. Same contrite spirit; faith yields obedience and lays aside lofty claims.

verses.text: He who kills an ox is as he who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, as he who breaks a dog’s neck; he who offers an offering, as he who offers pig’s blood; he who burns frankincense, as he who blesses an idol. Yes, they have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Solomon, Prov. 15:8, comments: the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord. The prophet is not reflecting upon idolatrous worship, but formal worship: those who in a formality worshipped the true God by acts which he had appointed. These services were no more acceptable than murder, idolatry, or the most horrid profanation of his name. Own ways—they live as they lust. Delight—they take pleasure in their sins.

They perform the appointed acts with wicked hearts. Altar; the church still refuses that delight. Shared ground with Calvin: they have chosen their own ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: all the sacrifices of the nation are of no value when they think God is satisfied with a deceitful appearance. He does not absolutely condemn sacrifices, but their blemishes. No sacrifices are acceptable but those which proceed from a pure heart. They mixed Gentile ceremonies with the Law. Streams from a muddy fountain cannot be clean. Choice and desire reveal obstinacy: they devoted their heart to what opposed his commandments.

The thing appointed, the heart refused. Same ox like a slain man; intention does not make invented or hollow worship clean.

verses.text: I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears on them, because when I called, no one answered; when I spoke, they didn’t listen, but they did that which was evil in my eyes, and chose that in which I didn’t delight.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: they have chosen to mock and delude me; I will chuse to suffer them to delude themselves; they have chosen to work wickedness, I will chuse the effect. Their fears—the things which they feared. Did not hear—God accounts that those do not hear who do not obey his will.

They could have answered; he called, they did not listen. Harsh treatment matches their choice. He is not surprised they refused. Judah; the church still hears when I called. Common reading: they chose that in which I didn’t delight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: I will choose their delusions—I will scatter the clouds they spread, so that their delusions shall be visible. I will bring upon them their terror. Because I called, and ye did not answer: they sinned through deliberate malice rather than ignorance; those to whom the word is proclaimed are condemned more severely. To hear is to obey. Before mine eyes they sinned as if to provoke him. He condemns foolish devotions, not only gross crimes.

The word was near; they shut the door. Same unanswered calling as 65:12; what they choose, he abhors.
verses.keyContrast: He called, they did not answer. Arminians hear Wesley’s permission: I will suffer them to delude themselves, and choose the effect of the wickedness they chose. Reformed Christians follow Calvin’s judicial exposing of delusions and bringing their terror, because they despised the word on purpose. Both confess: when I spoke, they didn’t listen; they chose what he did not delight in.

verses.text: Hear the LORD’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: you—that truly fear God. Your brethren—by nation. Cast you out—of their synagogues, of their city, and some of you out of the world. For my name’s sake—for your adherence to my law. Glorified—thinking they did God good service (John 16:2).

The small company that fears the word, hated by national brothers. Synagogue first; gospel church next. Either reading: they shall be put to shame.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he addresses the true worshippers, a small number, as formerly “bind the testimony among my disciples” (Isa 8:16). The mark is trembling at the word. He calls the mockers brethren by concession; this internal war with hypocrites is not new. Casting you out is tyranny of the many. Let Jehovah be glorified is their sneer or false confidence; he will be seen to your joy, and they shall blush.

God arms himself against enemies within the household of faith. Same cast-out remnant; God appears for believers’ advantage and the destruction of those who laughed.

verses.text: A voice of tumult from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of the LORD that repays his enemies what they deserve.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the expression of a prophetical ecstasy, as if he said, I hear a sad and affrighting noise; it comes not from the city only, but from the temple, wherein these formalists have so much gloried. There is a noise of soldiers slaying, and of the poor people shrieking. Of the Lord—not in thunder, but that rendereth recompence to his enemies. Thus he seems to express the destruction of the Jews by the Roman armies, as a thing at that time doing.

Temple, later Rome’s stroke, then any house that gloried in form. Shared ground with Calvin: recompense from the temple itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God hath not threatened in vain. It may relate to Babylon, whose destruction was the Church’s deliverance, but he is more favorable to domestic foes nourished in the Church’s bosom. From the temple, their lurking-place of false confidence, his voice shall come forth. A mitigation: the same terror may not discourage the believing servants of God.

An armed word where the mild word was scorned. Same uproar from the city; hypocrites shall hear a tumultuous voice, and believers receive the fruit of patience.
